title: Fallback commitments and customer scripting — trust-first incident positioning
summary: A compact GTM playbook focused on how Redwood frames graceful degradation and fallbacks to customers: commitments we can make, sample operator scripts for sales/CS/support, competitive differentiation, and canned customer communications for common incident patterns.
audience: sales, customer success, solutions engineering, product marketing, support
playbook:
Purpose
This is a go-to-market compendium for positioning Redwood when customers experience partial failures, latency spikes, or quality regressions. The goal: preserve trust by combining technical clarity, explicit commitments, and operational empathy. Keep language accessible for non-technical stakeholders while giving engineers clear fallback options to promise.

TL;DR messaging pillars
- Be transparent: tell customers what you know, what you don't, and expected next steps.
- Commit to a measurable mitigation and timeline (when possible) — e.g., rolling fallback in 5–15m for model variant, region failover in 10–30m.
- Offer options: degrade gracefully (reduced throughput or shorter context), fail to a guaranteed baseline model, or route to a cached response.
- Signal ownership: designate single point-of-contact and provide a short post-incident summary with actionable follow-ups.

Core commitments and precise language (phrases reps should use)
- "We’re prioritizing continuity: we will route requests to a lower-latency model variant to keep your operations online while we investigate the underlying cause."
- "We expect initial mitigation (fallback routing or reduced concurrency) within 10–20 minutes and a full diagnostic update within 2 business hours."
- "We’ll provide a post-incident report that includes root cause, customer impact, and compensatory credits if SLOs were missed."
- Avoid absolutes like "never" or "won't happen again". Prefer: "we will" + measurable time windows.

Incident scenarios, customer scripts, and operator actions
1) Short-term latency spike (hosted region)
- Symptoms: sudden token latency increase, elevated 95th/99th latency, no immediate errors.
- Customer-facing subject line: "Incident update: temporary latency spike; initial mitigation in progress"
- First-line CS script: "We’re seeing an elevated token latency in Region A affecting some customers. Our routing layer is shifting traffic to adjacent capacity while we identify the root cause. You should see latency return towards normal within the next 10–20 minutes for most requests. We’ll update you in 30 minutes or as we have new information."
- Engineering fallback options: enable model-variant downgrade (e.g., 16-bit quantized, smaller context), reduce max tokens, activate priority lanes for critical routes, enable prefix cache warming.
- Promises to make: timeline for mitigation (10–20m), offer to whitelist critical routes for priority lanes, provide a brief post-incident timeline.

2) Partial region outage (networking or infra)
- Symptoms: region health checks failing, elevated 5xx rates for region-specific endpoints.
- Customer-facing subject line: "Service continuity update: regional disruption & failover plan"
- CS script: "Our control plane has detected degraded capacity in Region A. We are failing over affected customers to Region B; requests will continue to be served but may see small latency changes. If your regulatory constraints require Region A only, we will coordinate a targeted remediation plan and provide an ETA for restoration."
- Engineering fallback options: automated multi-region failover (when enabled), per-tenant routing override to safe regions, temporary model variant swap to a smaller GPU shape that is available in target region.
- Promises to make: explicit reorder — what will change (latency, watermarking), how long to expect the fallback (estimate), and whether any data residency exceptions apply.

3) Model quality regression (generation drift / hallucination spike)
- Symptoms: elevated rejection/qa regressions, regression alerts triggered by evals or customer reports.
- Customer-facing subject line: "Quality alert: temporary model regression and mitigation steps"
- CS script: "We’ve detected an increase in outputs that don’t meet expected quality. We’re routing your traffic to a verified fallback model that preserves intent with reduced hallucination risk. Our team is investigating the rollout differences that caused this and will keep you updated."
- Engineering fallback options: pin to previous model version, route to conservative decoding settings (higher logprob thresholds, lower temperature), enable targeted prompt-rewrites or safety filters, temporarily disable risky generation endpoints.
- Promises: immediate fallback within X minutes, remediation plan with timeline for revalidation and reassessment before re-rolling the updated model.

Canned customer messages (templates)
1) Short email update (first 30 minutes)
Subject: Incident update: brief latency spike in Region A
Hi <Customer>,
We’re currently investigating a temporary latency spike in Region A affecting some requests. We’re shifting traffic to neighboring capacity to reduce impact and expect visible improvement within 10–20 minutes.
Named contact: <SRE/CS rep>. We’ll follow up in 30 minutes or sooner with more details.
Thanks for your patience,
<Redwood team>

2) Post-incident summary (24–48 hours)
Subject: Post-incident summary: Region A latency spike — root cause & actions
Hi <Customer>,
Thanks for your patience while we investigated the Region A incident on <date>. Summary: cause, mitigation steps taken, customer impact (approx. % of requests affected and duration), permanent mitigations (code, infra, process changes), and any credits applied. Action items and owner are listed below.
Regards,
<Redwood ops>

Competitive notes — how to differentiate in conversations
- Against managed cloud endpoints that lack multi-region routing: highlight Redwood’s routing policies and automatic safe-fallbacks that preserve availability without customer involvement. "With Redwood, you get active multi-region routing and automated model fallbacks so your app keeps answering users even when a single region degrades."
- Against DIY/self-hosted inference: emphasize SLO-backed operational playbooks, clear transparency commitments, and the tools for quick rollbacks and canaries. "You could build this yourself, but you’d lose months of operational hardening and the playbooks we use to keep production systems stable under load."
- Against providers pushing only always-upgrading models: stress the importance of pinned versions and conservative QA rollouts. "We allow conservative pins and gradual rollouts so you never wake up to a silent regression in the chain."

Objection handling snippets for sales/CS
- "Can you guarantee zero downtime?" -> "No provider can realistically promise zero downtime; what we guarantee is predictable mitigation: time-boxed fallbacks, transparent root-cause reports, and credits tied to SLO misses. That predictability is what keeps customer applications resilient."
- "Why not always run the fastest model?" -> "We optimize for economic and quality trade-offs: for critical paths we recommend pinned, validated models with fallback variants that reduce both cost and risk during incidents."

Launch checklist (what GTM should verify before promoting messaging)
- Confirm standard fallback timelines with SRE (minutes for routing change, hours for deeper remediation).
- Validate canned email templates with legal and trust teams.
- Ensure CS has dashboard access to per-tenant routing overrides.
- Prepare an internal quick-reference one-pager for sales (one sheet: responses to top 6 customer questions).

Operational signals to track (metrics to feed into messaging)
- Percent of requests served by fallback model (by tenant and region).
- Time-to-first-mitigation (median, 95th).
- Post-incident NPS change and ticket reopen rate.
- SLO breach frequency and cumulative minutes of degraded service per month.

Open questions / decisions for leadership
- Standard crediting policy thresholds (when does an SLO miss trigger a credit and what type: bill credit vs free capacity?).
- Formalizing timelines we can safely promise across Dedicated and Private customers (private deployments may have constraints).
- Whether to expose an API-level flag customers can set to prefer latency over quality (and the default).

Appendix: quick operator runbook bullets (internal)
- If 95th latency > baseline * 3: flip canary to fallback model (ops flag: fallback-mode=on), reduce batch size for affected routes.
- If region healthchecks fail: start automated failover to paired region, notify CS with template, start RCA channel.
- If quality regression alert: pin all traffic to previous model version and freeze rollouts until manual QA pass.

Conclusion
This doc is intended as a living playbook. Push updates after each real incident — add customer language that worked (or didn’t), update timelines validated by SRE, and capture any new fallback primitives the runtime team adds. The combination of pragmatic fallbacks + clear, measured language is our strongest GTM signal for reliability and trust.
